# The sngl:time clock and instant arithmetic, run as compiled Go and then run
# again on the interpreter.
#
# testdata/time_clock_arithmetic.txtar says what each target generates; this
# says the answers agree. Two runners over one program is the claim that
# matters here, because the two carry a datetime differently -- Go as a
# time.Time and the interpreter as the ISO string a literal is written in --
# and a conversion that is wrong in one of them is invisible from the other.
#
# Nothing here asserts an absolute instant, so the answers do not depend on
# when the suite ran. The two that do read the clock are bounded rather than
# exact: each reads it twice and a real clock has moved between the readings,
# which the truncating cast shows as 89 rather than 90.
#
# `since` and `until` have SNGL bodies calling `between` and `now` by their
# bare names, which only library source can write. Nothing dispatched an
# #[intrinsic] reached that way in the interpreter, so both evaluated to null
# in silence; `elapsed` and `left` are what say they do not.
#
# `ratio` is duration / duration, which the checker types as a float. Go
# carries a duration as an integer time.Duration and Kotlin as a Long, so both
# divided as integers -- Go returning one from a float64 function, which does
# not compile at all.

sngl test --platform=bubbletea --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

sngl test --platform=none app.sngl
stdout 'PASS'
! stdout 'FAIL'

-- app.sngl --
import . "sngl:test"
import ui "sngl:ui"
import time "sngl:time"

component main ui.node {
    var anchor time.datetime = "2024-01-15T10:30:00"
    var period time.duration = 250ms
    var ahead = 0
    var behind = 0
    var left = 0
    var elapsed = 0
    var ratio = 0.0
    var halved = 0

    effect(@mount {
        ahead = int(time.between(anchor, anchor.add(90s)) / 1s)
        behind = int(time.between(anchor.add(90s), anchor) / 1s)
        left = int(time.until(time.now().add(90s)) / 1s)
        elapsed = int(time.since(time.now().add(90s)) / 1s)
        ratio = time.duration(1m) / period
        halved = int((period / 2) / 1ms)
    })

    ui.text(value="{ahead}")
}

// An instant plus a duration is that far ahead of the instant it came from,
// and `between` reports the gap in the order its parameters name. Anchored on
// a literal rather than on the clock, so the two runners answer exactly: two
// readings of a real clock differ by the time between them, and the truncating
// cast turns that into 89.
func testAnAddedDurationIsTheGap(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.ahead == 90)
}

// The same gap read the other way round is negative. A duration carries a
// sign like any other magnitude, which is what lets `until` report an instant
// that has already passed.
func testTheReverseGapIsNegative(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.behind == -90)
}

// `until` and `since` are the two halves of `between` with `now` supplied, so
// they answer the same number with opposite signs. Bounded rather than exact,
// because each reads the clock a second time and a real one has moved.
func testUntilAndSinceAreOpposites(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.left >= 89 && c.left <= 90)
    t.assert(c.elapsed >= -90 && c.elapsed <= -89)
}

// duration / duration is the dimensionless ratio of the two magnitudes, and a
// float: 1m over 250ms is 240 whichever representation the target carries.
func testTheRatioOfTwoDurationsIsAFloat(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.ratio == 240.0)
}

// duration / number is still a duration, which is the other half of the same
// rule and the one that has always worked.
func testADurationOverANumberIsADuration(t Test, c main) {
    t.assert(c.halved == 125)
}

ui.window {
    main
}
